title: Effects of Orthotic Interventions on Pain, Balance, and Plantar Pressure in Flexible Flatfoot: A Systematic Review

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Effects of Orthotic Interventions on Pain, Balance, and Plantar Pressure in Flexible Flatfoot: A Systematic Review》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · jfa270218-sec-0010-p3】Pain is a key outcome because it directly affects patients' daily functioning and quality of life [11]. Individuals with flexible flat feet often report various pain patterns, including arch pain, heel pain, and general foot fatigue. Balance is a second relevant outcome, because the altered foot posture can reduce proprioceptive input from the plantar surface and impair postural control [12, 13]. Studies have shown that individual with flexible flatfoot exhibit greater postural sway and compromised stability compared with those with normal foot arches [14, 15]. Plantar pressure measurement provides an objective way to quantify how flatfoot and its treatment alter foot loading.

【Introduction · jfa270218-sec-0010-p5】Therefore, this study aims to systematically review the effects of orthotic interventions on pain, balance, and plantar pressure distribution in individuals with flexible flatfoot. By synthesizing evidence across these three critical outcome domains, this review aims to inform the clinical management of flexible flatfoot and to identify gaps for further research.

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Effects of Orthotic Interventions on Pain, Balance, and Plantar Pressure in Flexible Flatfoot: A Systematic Review》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Study Design · jfa270218-sec-0030-p1】A systematic review was performed following PRISMA guidelines [16]. The protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD42025649490). No amendment to the registered protocol was filed while the review was being conducted; an amendment recording the deviations declared in this manuscript, including those introduced at revision, has since been filed with the PROSPERO registry; the narrowing of the plantar variable to peak pressure, declared below, will be added at the next update of that record. Three procedures specified in the protocol were not carried out as planned: screening of the reference lists of included reports, the pre‐specified subgroup and meta‐regression analyses, and the planned pooling of effect estimates within each outcome domain. Each deviation is described in the sections below. The search was run to October 16, 2025 rather than to the February 16, 2025 date named in the protocol; the protocol provided for the search to be updated before the final analysis, so this is an update rather than a departure. The appraisal of nonrandomized studies with ROBINS‐I was specified in the protocol and is not a deviation either. The eligibility criteria are otherwise those of the protocol, with the design descriptions in criteria (1) and (4) made explicit at revision to name a within‐subject design that was included but not named in the protocol. This study examined the biomechanical and clinical impacts of orthotic interventions on the flexible flatfoot, focusing on pain, balance, and plantar pressure distribution.

【Study Designs and Their Designation · jfa270218-sec-0070-p1】The eight included studies do not share one design, and the collective label “controlled trials” used in earlier versions of this manuscript did not describe all of them accurately. Six studies allocated participants at random. Five of these allocated participants to parallel groups [17, 18, 19, 20, 21]; in the sixth [22] each participant was measured under every condition and only the order of the conditions was randomized. One of the five [18] ran parallel groups to 6 months and then crossed participants over, so only its first period would have been eligible had it contributed an estimate. One study allocated participants to parallel groups by patient preference rather than at random [23]. One recruited by non‐random convenience sampling and compared orthotic conditions within the same participants, each participant serving as his or her own control [24]; that design is not a controlled trial in the parallel‐group sense at all. Neither is the condition‐order design of [22], although that study did randomize. We therefore no longer apply a single collective label to all eight. They are referred to collectively as the included studies, and the design of each is named wherever its design bears on the analysis, as a randomized controlled trial, a nonrandomized controlled trial, or a within‐subject repeated‐measures study. Retaining a label broad enough to cover all eight would have concealed precisely the design differences that determine which risk‐of‐bias instrument applies, whether a contrast is paired or unpaired, and how much weight the resulting estimate can carry.

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Effects of Orthotic Interventions on Pain, Balance, and Plantar Pressure in Flexible Flatfoot: A Systematic Review》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Results · jfa270218-sec-0160-p1】The systematic search yielded 290 articles. After removing 45 duplicates and screening 245 records, 59 articles underwent full‐text assessment. Eight studies met all inclusion criteria for final analysis, including a total of 382 unique participants with flexible flatfoot: Taspinar et al. [23] (n = 60), Yurt et al. [21] (n = 67), Elsayed et al. [20] (n = 40), Liebau et al. [18] (n = 52), Saeedi et al. [22] (n = 34), Yalfani et al. [17] (n = 30), Khodaei et al. [24] (n = 19), and Xu et al. [19] (n = 80). Two of these studies did not allocate participants at random: Taspinar et al. [23] reported that their three groups could not be randomized and assigned participants according to patient preference, and Khodaei et al. [24] used non‐random convenience sampling. Following independent re‐verification of every effect size, no outcome domain could be pooled. Each domain is now represented by a single study, and all pooled estimates, all heterogeneity statistics, and all summary diamonds reported in the previous version are withdrawn. Where a study contributed more than one eligible arm or more than one eligible measure within a domain, those data were either combined into one estimate or a single dataset was carried forward, so that no participant is now represented more than once within any analysis and the unit‐of‐analysis violation present in the previous version is removed. Publication bias could not be formally assessed using funnel plots or Egger's test due to insufficient studies (< 10) per outcome domain.

【Conclusion · jfa270218-sec-0290-p1】This systematic review found that the available studies cannot be pooled. Independent re‐verification withdrew every pooled estimate reported in the previous version, and each outcome domain now rests on a single study. Against a comparator providing no arch support, one trial showed a large reduction in pain (g = −1.017, 95% CI −1.54 to −0.49) on its own designated primary instrument. The same trial's Foot Function Index total gives g = −0.28, so the magnitude of that benefit is unstable. Adding short foot exercise to an orthosis worn by both arms reduced pain in one further trial (g = −0.974, 95% CI −1.62 to −0.33). That result concerns the exercise rather than the device. One trial showed better dynamic balance at 12 weeks with the orthosis removed (g = −0.859, 95% CI −1.59 to −0.13). One within‐subject study showed that orthoses redistribute plantar load away from the heel and lesser metatarsals and toward the medial midfoot. That redistribution is the mechanical action such devices are designed to produce, and it is the most consistent finding in this review. Taken together, the corrected evidence supports the mechanical action of foot orthoses better than it supports any specific clinical benefit. Orthoses remain a reasonable conservative option for flexible flatfoot, but the size of their effect on pain and balance is not established. Adequately powered randomized trials with comparable outcomes and clearly defined comparators are required.
